flow: Mean two-year change in family wealth per adult, active vs passive (GBP, excl DB pensions and pensions in payment); active, passive: 2008-10 +11k,-9k; 2010-12 +1k,+5k; 2012-14 +12k,about 0 (no label); 2014-16 +10k,+11k; 2016-18 +3k,+19k; 2018-20 +13k,+8k; 2020-22 +8k,+12k
population: Mean per adult family (benefit unit), GB
what_it_mixes: Total change includes DC pension and passive gains on them; DB pensions and pensions in payment excluded (p22 note). Active is a residual: saving, debt change and transfers
by_band_age_income: None: all adults; no band split
held_as_data: No: RF analysis, not in 097r or 098r. WAS Table 2.1 aggregates are held but not this split
note: Values read from the printed bar labels (image checked). 2012-14 passive bar carries no label

flow: Passive share of growth in average family wealth: 53% since 2010-12 (active 47%); latest period 2018-20 to 2020-22 passive 60%, active 40%
what_it_mixes: As BF-01 (DB pensions excluded, so true passive share likely higher, p21 fn19)
note: Cross-check from BF-01 labels: passive 55k of 102k = 54% over 2010-12 to 2020-22; consistent

flow: Median two-year passive asset-price return 2018-20 to 2020-22: about 8% for the middle wealth quintile, zero for the bottom quintile; wide gap between 25th and 75th percentile (Fig 9, chart without values)
population: Families by net wealth quintile, GB
what_it_mixes: Asset-price return on opening holdings only; excludes DB pensions and pensions in payment
by_band_age_income: Wealth quintiles (not pack deciles, not WAS GBP bands)
note: Two-year return, not annual. Not turned into a rate. Housing 40% of wealth in 6th decile, 29% in top quintile (p23 fn23)

flow: Table 1: mobility of age-adjusted per-adult wealth, 2016-18 to two years later and four years later. Low-to-middle income / higher income. Correlation 78/78 and 75/72%; rank correlation 79/74 and 81/77%; stay in same decile 43/33 and 43/32%; same decile or one either side 82/76 and 83/73%; rise in rank 29/40 and 32/45%; fall in rank 29/27 and 25/22% (two years/four years)
population: Individuals aged 25-54 in 2016-18, benefit-unit wealth per adult, GB
what_it_mixes: Total net wealth including pensions; age-adjusted
by_band_age_income: Age-adjusted wealth deciles within the sample (not pack deciles, not WAS GBP bands)
stage_definition: None; ages 25-54 only, so working-age cells only

validation_moment_096r: band transition matrix; share with falling wealth

flow: Mean change in wealth 2016-18 to 2018-20 / 2020-22 (March 2025 prices, CPIH): age-adjusted low-to-middle -6,000 / -30,700, higher +5,200 / +26,400; unadjusted low-to-middle +33,600 / +68,500, higher +45,300 / +128,200
population: Individuals aged 25-54 in 2016-18, per-adult benefit-unit wealth
what_it_mixes: Total net wealth including pension accrual
by_band_age_income: Income group (low-to-middle vs higher), not wealth band
validation_moment_096r: share with falling wealth (mean change by income group)
note: Mean, not share. Unadjusted figures include life-cycle accumulation

flow: Share remaining in the same wealth decile four years later: 27% for higher-income aged 25-34 and 34% for those aged 35-54 (text); Fig 22 bars also give the within-one-decile shares by age and income
what_it_mixes: Total net wealth
note: Only the higher-income figures are stated in text; the low-to-middle bars are chart labels with ambiguous mapping in extracted text, so not recorded

flow: Rank change 2016-18 to 2020-22: at the 25th percentile of wealth higher-income families end on average 2.5 rank points higher than low-to-middle; at the 75th percentile 6.5 points; average gap in expected rank about 20 points across all
what_it_mixes: Total net wealth
note: Regression-based rank gaps, not transition probabilities

flow: Composition among 40-44 year olds, 2016-18: pensions 36% of total wealth (higher income) vs 31% (low-to-middle); net housing 31% vs 28%
what_it_mixes: Pension wealth included (valuation not stated here)
note: Composition only

flow: Liquid savings: share of non-pensioner families with at least 1,000 pounds liquid: bottom income quintile 35% (2019-20) to 44% (2021-22); top quintile 89% to 91%. Median change in liquid savings 2019-20 to 2021-22: top quintile 4,200 (text p32; p29 says 4,100), second quintile above 300 vs 100 before, bottom quintile no typical improvement; 10% of bottom quintile lost 4,000 or more
what_it_mixes: Liquid assets only (current accounts, savings, ISAs, NS&I, cash); no pension, no housing, no debt
held_as_data: No. Not comparable with ONS saving ratio (held in 097r ons_household_flows_annual.csv): this is a stock change in liquid assets
note: Pandemic period; not a saving rate. Internal inconsistency 4,100 vs 4,200 noted

flow: Share increasing liquid savings 2019-20 to 2021-22: 55% bottom income quintile, 64% top; 34% to 40% in each quintile reported a decline
what_it_mixes: Liquid savings only
note: Compares WAS with pandemic-era YouGov surveys; different survey bases

flow: Aggregate: household wealth 17 trillion pounds in 2020-22 (property 5.5 trillion, 32%; pensions 8.2 trillion, 48%); 11.2 trillion in 2006-08 (property 42%, pensions 37%); about 7.5 times GDP in 2020-22, about 3 times in mid-1980s; DB pension valuation difference 2.9 trillion
what_it_mixes: Pension wealth on the RF valuation (market annuity rates, not ONS SCAPE rates)
held_as_data: Yes: WAS Table 2.1 in data/rates/totalwealthtables.xlsx gives 13,568bn total, 5,461bn property, 4,808bn pension for the same round (ONS SCAPE basis). Property matches RF 5.5tn; pension differs by RF's own DB valuation (p15, Annex 1). RF 7.5x GDP equals the high end of I-D4a. Price bases may also differ (RF adjusts to 2020-22 prices with CPIH); not reconciled here
note: Do not mix the two pension valuations in one validation

flow: Mean per-adult family wealth 2020-22 (RF basis, 2020-22 prices): 168k overall; by wealth decile 1k, 14k, 32k, 69k, 129k, 212k, 310k, 452k, 691k, 1.5m; top decile more than 11 times the fifth
population: Per-adult family wealth by wealth decile, GB
what_it_mixes: Pension wealth on the RF valuation
by_band_age_income: Per-adult family wealth deciles (not the pack's household deciles)
held_as_data: Partly: ons_was_wealth_by_age_of_hrp.csv and WAS Table 2.5 are household-based, ONS pension basis; not directly comparable
note: Per adult in a benefit unit vs per household in the held tables

flow: Concentration: top 10% hold about half of wealth consistently since 1980; WAS missed about 5% of total wealth (about 800bn) in 2016-18, which would lift the top 1% share from 18% to 23% (citing Advani, Bangham and Leslie 2020); wealth Gini 0.70 in 2020-22; 90th to 50th percentile ratio 5.2
what_it_mixes: Net total wealth
held_as_data: Yes: I-D4d (18.0 central, 23.0 high) and I-D4e (5.0) in docs/model-v3/inputs.md agree
note: Same upstream source as the register (S5); not new evidence

flow: Age and stage context 2020-22: people aged 60 and over held 49% of wealth (39% in 2006-08), 53% of property, 59% of financial, 45% of pension wealth; passive gain largest at 75-79 (nearly 18,000, 2018-20 to 2020-22), about 9,000 in the late 30s; Fig 11 bars (no labels) show active accumulation dominating under 60 and passive dominating over 60, and negative active (drawdown) at ages 70 and over in 2016-18 and 2020-22
what_it_mixes: Excludes DB pensions and pensions in payment from passive; total includes DC
stage_definition: Age proxy for stage; retired not identified
held_as_data: Partly: ons_was_wealth_by_age_of_hrp.csv has components by age of household reference person (household basis, ONS pension basis); persons-by-age-by-band in was_persons_age_by_wealth_band.csv
validation_moment_096r: retired financial wealth change (qualitative: negative active at 70+)
note: Chart bars carry no values; only the text figures are recorded as numbers. Retired and stage are not defined: age groups only

flow: Adjusted household saving ratio peaked at 25% in Q2 2020; stock of household savings rose by 137bn pounds in real terms Apr 2020 to Mar 2022 (Bank of England Bankstats); ratio excludes pension equity adjustment and includes NPISH
what_it_mixes: Ratio excludes adjustment for pension equity (p30 note)
held_as_data: Yes (annual only): 097r qsa_household_annual_2026q2.csv, sheet HH_3 series DGD8, households saving ratio 16.5% in 2020 and 5.7% in 2019 (annual, total ratio incl. pension adjustment); the RF quarterly adjusted ratio (25% peak) is a different, seasonally adjusted measure and is not in the held annual CSV
note: Quarterly peak; the held series is annual. Adjusted saving ratio is not the ONS total ratio that is half pension (097r s9)

flow: Share of the average two-year change in family FINANCIAL wealth explained by asset prices and yields (counterfactual from class returns on opening holdings); residual is net saving. 2008-10 to 2010-12 93%; 2010-12 to 2012-14 93%; 2012-14 to 2014-16 82%; 2014-16 to 2016-18 76%; 2016-18 79%
what_it_mixes: Financial wealth only (net of other financial liabilities); pensions, property and debt secured on property are not in it
held_as_data: No. Source is Bangham and Leslie 2020 (not held). Same method as the Before the fall RF split (BF-01, BF-02) but financial wealth only and an older period
note: Bar labels read from the page image. The chart plots five bars; the text names only the first (93%, p15). Passive share = price and yield effect; the rest is net saving, not a saving rate

flow: Two-year mobility: 80% of families in the top wealth decile stay in it; about 90% of entrants come from the ninth decile; 7% of families in the bottom half move into the top half
population: Families linked between two WAS rounds, GB
years: 2014-16 to 2016-18 (Fig 13 note); the text says 2014-16 base on PDF 4 and 2016-18 base on PDF 23
what_it_mixes: Total net wealth including pensions, business and physical wealth
by_band_age_income: Family net wealth deciles and halves (not pack deciles, not WAS GBP bands)
validation_moment_096r: band transition matrix (top decile row only); share with falling wealth (not given)
note: Only the top-decile stay rate and the half-to-half move are stated; the full Fig 13 matrix is a chart without numbers in the text. The paper dates the same statistic 2014-16 on PDF 4 and 2016-18 on PDF 23: recorded as stated, not reconciled

flow: A median household saving all disposable income would need over 400 years to move from median wealth to the average wealth of the richest 1%; median net disposable household income about 23,000 pounds in 2018-19
what_it_mixes: Disposable income only; wealth basis the paper's WAS total
note: A rhetorical comparison, not a saving rate or an accumulation estimate

flow: Aggregate GB financial wealth up more than 60% in real terms from 1.4 trillion pounds (2006-08) to 2.3 trillion (CPI-adjusted); described as driven overwhelmingly by asset prices rather than active saving (Bangham and Leslie 2020, Mulheirn 2020)
what_it_mixes: Financial wealth, net of financial liabilities; pensions excluded
held_as_data: Partly: data/rates/totalwealthtables.xlsx holds financial net 1,915bn for 2020-22 (R8), a different round, so no direct duplicate
note: Price basis is the paper's CPI adjustment; the cited decomposition is not held

flow: Share of financial wealth held in zero-return assets (cash, current accounts) by family net wealth decile, mean shares: 71, 57, 54, 47, 44, 38, 32, 27, 23, 17 (deciles 1 to 10, lowest labelled first in the chart; the paper drops negative net wealth in the lowest decile per the Fig 4 note, Fig 5 carries ten bars)
what_it_mixes: Financial wealth only
note: Shows return heterogeneity by band (risky and safe shares are the other segments, not recorded because the segment labels are ambiguous in the image). The lowest-decile note is on PDF 14 under Fig 4 and may not apply to Fig 5

flow: Illustration: with a 4% return on wealth a 1% wealth tax equals a 25% tax on the flow of capital income; elasticities also restated at 4.5% and 3% returns
what_it_mixes: Not stated
note: Assumed returns used for arithmetic. Not measured; no UK band-level return or saving share anywhere in the paper

flow: Chetty et al. (2014): 15% of the population are active savers who shift saving into retirement accounts while total saving is unchanged
what_it_mixes: Pension saving shifted, total unchanged
note: Second-hand citation; not a UK moment

flow: Saving responses to wealth taxes: Brulhart et al. (2021) Switzerland, saving the mechanical tax saving would explain 5.7% of the aggregate taxable wealth response, observed saving explains 4.3%; Seim (2017) Sweden and Ring (2020) Norway quoted qualitatively (Ring: positive effect on yearly saving)
what_it_mixes: Taxable wealth response, not a household saving rate
note: Not UK. The paper states minimal evidence of reduced saving (PDF 2). These are behavioural-response shares, not saving or depletion rates

flow: Realised capital gains: more than 90% of all taxable gains go to individuals with total remuneration (taxable income plus realised gains) above 100,000 pounds; the top 1% of incomes (above 125,000) receive an average 47,000 pounds of gains on top of income (Advani and Summers 2020)
population: UK individuals with income or remuneration above 100,000
years: Tax years 2007-08 to 2017-18 (data); gains figures as cited
what_it_mixes: Realised gains only; accrued and unrealised gains are omitted (PDF 4, 6)
by_band_age_income: Remuneration rank, not wealth band; no wealth-band share
held_as_data: No (HMRC SPI-based; 097r hmrc_csv holds other series)
note: A tax-rank statistic. No band-level share of top-tail wealth from gains

flow: Mean effective average tax rate on income plus realised gains peaks at 38% at 500,000 pounds remuneration and falls below 30% above 3 million; 23bn pounds static revenue if income above 100,000 paid headline rates
what_it_mixes: Realised gains; income tax and CGT
note: Tax paid on realised flows. Not a return, saving or accrual rate. The US top-25 figures (3.4%, PDF 2) are not UK and are not recorded as moments

flow: Households and wealth above thresholds in 2026: above 50m pounds 1,710 households 695.9bn; above 100m 946, 642.5bn; above 250m 444, 566.2bn; above 1,000m 129, 417.5bn. Pareto coefficient 0.91 fitted to Rich List resident entries ranked 50 to 287; HMRC (Davies 2025) counts 2,500 individuals above 100m and 5,000 above 50m, quoted as 1,086 and 2,171 households
what_it_mixes: Net worth as the Rich List measures it; method not a WAS pension basis
by_band_age_income: Fixed GBP thresholds from 50m; far above the top WAS band and the pack's top decile (top 1% and above)
held_as_data: Partly: docs/model-v3/inputs.md I-D4f (Rich List 2026, 350 entries, 784bn) is the same list source (S7, read via High Pay Centre); the paper uses 287 resident entries and 522bn for the top 300 households (PDF 19), so the totals differ by population (residents only, households not entries). Not reconciled
note: A UK band-level count and wealth, but only for the extreme tail, and a Pareto extrapolation plus Rich List. Not a saving, return or gains split

flow: Aggregate wealth of the top 181 resident Rich List entries grew 6.48% per year (nominal) 2016 to 2026; used to grow the top-tail 10 years; top 300 resident households 522bn in 2026 and 800bn in 2036 on that trend
population: Top 181 resident Rich List entries; top 300 households
what_it_mixes: Not stated; includes price changes, saving, transfers, entries and exits together
note: Nominal, aggregate and membership changes year to year (the top 181 resident entries are taken each year, so members change). Not a return, saving rate or gains share and not converted into one. The paper assumes no entry or exit in the projection

flow: Global billionaire wealth grew 7.1% per year real, 1987 to 2024 (Forbes); with a 0.3% capital tax and consumption of 0.1% of wealth this implies a gross return of 7.5%. Average global pre-tax return 6-7%, of which pure capital gains about 2% (Bauluz, Novokmet and Schularick 2022) and business-level capital taxes close to 1%
population: Global billionaires and the global average
what_it_mixes: Total return including capital gains; consumption is an assumed 0.1% of wealth, not measured
note: Not UK. A decomposition of top-tail growth into return, tax and consumption that rests on an assumed consumption share. The UK is not covered (the one UK mention, PDF 9, is a citation)

source: Tax by Design (Adam et al. 2011; book page = PDF - 14)
flow: Share of gross financial wealth held in private pensions, ISAs-PEPs-TESSAs and other assets by gross financial wealth decile, benefit units with a member aged 52-64: pensions 12.6, 54.8, 65.2, 68.2, 69.7, 74.7, 78.1, 81.8, 79.0, 68.4% (deciles 1 to 10), all 73.6%; ISAs 5.5%; other 20.9%. Decile bounds from under 1.7k to over 511.2k pounds
population: Benefit units with a member aged 52-64, England
what_it_mixes: Private pension wealth includes DC fund value and accrued DB entitlements; non-housing; gross financial wealth
by_band_age_income: Deciles of gross financial wealth (not pack deciles, not WAS bands)
held_as_data: No (ELSA, old vintage; ELSA is not held)
note: A stock composition, not a flow

flow: Composition of estates passing on death 2007-08 by estate size: all 270,639 estates residential 52%, cash 24%, securities 14%, other 10%; above 2m pounds 1,443 estates residential 25%, cash 12%, securities 35%, other 29%
population: Estates notified for probate, UK (about half of estates excluded)
what_it_mixes: Assets at death; no pensions
note: Composition at death only; no flow

flow: Household saving rate (including NPISH) 10.8% in Q2 2025, up 7 percentage points from 4.0% in 2022, the rise focused in cash saving rather than pensions
what_it_mixes: Total saving ratio; the text implies pension saving is a separate, smaller part of the rise
held_as_data: Yes (annual): 097r qsa_household_annual_2026q2.csv HH_3 DGD8 5.0% in 2022 and 9.6% in 2025; HH_Alt CSJ8 0.8% and 7.8%. The report's 4.0% (2022) and 10.8% (Q2 2025) do not match the annual figures: the report does not say if 4.0% is a quarter, and Q2 is a single quarter (vintage and frequency differ)
note: Total ratio is roughly half pension (097r s9); this source does not split it

flow: Barclays-based forecast: household saving rate falls gradually to about 9% by 2030, against 7.2% in the OBR March 2025 EFO; Fig 1.3 is a chart without values
what_it_mixes: Same total ratio as GB-01
note: A forecast, not a moment to calibrate

flow: Top 1% share of total wealth in 2016-18: 14.4% on survey aggregates, 16.5% on national-accounts aggregates (2.1pp apart); over 2006 to 2018 the top 1% share lies between 12% and 18% and is 2.1 to 3.3pp higher on national-accounts aggregates
what_it_mixes: Net wealth; unfunded DB excluded in the main estimate (PDF 9), so the pension basis differs from WAS
by_band_age_income: Top 1% of individuals; not a pack decile or WAS band
held_as_data: Yes: docs/model-v3/inputs.md I-D4d top-1% share 14.4 / 18.0 / 23.0, whose low value 14.4 is this paper's survey-aggregate figure (S6) and whose central 18.0 is WAS as published (S5) and high 23.0 the missing-tail adjustment. The paper's own 16.5% sits between low and central
note: Aggregates choice, not a saving or return split. Survey versus national-accounts aggregates, not a saving or return split
